title: Yom Kippur: the gates close
hook: the day opens with Kol Nidre and ends as the gates of prayer close

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yom Kippur: twenty-five hours of fasting, standing like angels, after first making peace with the people you hurt. Your line was lighter for a day. What comfort did you set down? Day one hundred twenty-six.

Yom Kippur opens with a melody and closes with a horn. It begins at sunset. The synagogue is packed. The Torah scrolls are taken out and held. And a cantor sings a haunting old melody, three times, each time a little louder: Kol Nidre. Then, a whole day later, as the light starts to fade and everyone is hungry, tired, and still standing, the last prayer of the day begins. The doors of the ark stay open. People who sat through the afternoon get to their feet. They know what time it is.
screen: `SUNSET: KOL NIDRE, THREE TIMES.` → `A WHOLE DAY OF PRAYER.` → `THE LIGHT STARTS TO FADE.`

segments.voice: First, the opening. Kol Nidre means all vows. It isn't really a prayer; it's a legal formula, in Aramaic, releasing the vows a person makes to God and can't keep. Jewish law is clear that it doesn't cancel promises made to other people; those have to be kept or made right with the person. What gives it its power is the melody and the moment: a whole community admitting that people promise more than they manage. Now the end. The final service of Yom Kippur is called Neilah. The word means locking, or closing. The rabbis remembered that in the Temple, a closing prayer was said as the great gates were locked at sunset. And they also spoke of the gates of heaven, open all day to prayer, now swinging shut. So Neilah feels like the last minutes before a door closes. All through these days, the prayers have asked God to write us in the book of life. In Neilah, the word changes: seal us. The writing is almost done. Then the ending comes all at once. The whole congregation says the Shema, once. Then, three times, the line that follows it, blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom for ever and ever. Then, seven times, the words the people cried out on Mount Carmel in Elijah's day: "The LORD, He is God." And one long blast of the shofar. The fast is over. Many say next year in Jerusalem, and go home to eat. That closes a week that ran through the bedtime Shema, the calendar, the new moon, the shofar, the river, the fast, and now the gates.
screen: `KOL NIDRE: ALL VOWS.` · `NEILAH: THE GATES ARE CLOSING.` · `WRITE US, THEN SEAL US.` · `THE SHEMA, AND ONE LONG BLAST.` · then, large: `THE LORD, HE IS GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: end today with one quiet sentence. For now, rehearse it. Settle, and breathe. Imagine the day is almost over and the gates are closing. What's the one thing you'd still want to say? To God, if you pray. To someone you love. To yourself. Keep it to one sentence. Let it get simpler with each breath, until it's only a few words. Tonight, before you sleep, say it. The bell holds the time.
Neilah. The closing: the last prayer of Yom Kippur, said as the gates close, ending with the Shema and one long blast.
Your line: before the gates close. Today, don't leave the important sentence for tomorrow; say it while the day is still open. Day one hundred twenty-six.

original.note: Hebrew: locking, closing; the final prayer of Yom Kippur.

trapdoor: what you thought: the last service before everyone goes home to eat.
what it means: the closing of the gates, when the year's prayers are sealed and the day ends in the Shema and a shofar blast.
what a scholar hears: the Talmud debates whether neilah means the closing of the Temple gates or the gates of heaven; Kol Nidre is an Aramaic annulment of vows to God, never of promises to people.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of 1 Kings 18:39 ('The LORD, He is God; the LORD, He is God').
Neilah as Temple gates vs. gates of heaven: Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 4:1. Confirm citation.
Kol Nidre: an Aramaic annulment of personal vows to God, not obligations to others; historically misrepresented by opponents of Jews. Keeper to confirm the framing is careful and accurate.
Ending order (Shema once, Baruch shem three times, 'The LORD, He is God' seven times, shofar) is the widespread Ashkenazi and Sephardi practice; confirm.
